title: Quaker silence
hook: Quakers gather in silence and speak only when moved, seeking "that of God in every one" (George Fox)
carry: that of god in every one

segments.voice: Yesterday, centering prayer: one sacred word and a lot of gentle returning. Your line was consent. Where did you manage one quiet yes to something you didn't plan? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-seven.

Benches facing each other. No altar up front, no pulpit, nobody in robes. People come in, sit down, and say nothing. A long quiet stretch goes by. A cough. A chair creaks. Then a woman near the window stands up, says a few sentences about her father, and sits down again. Nobody replies. The silence closes back over, like water. More quiet. Then, at some point, two people shake hands, and everyone turns and shakes hands, and that's the service. This is a Quaker meeting for worship, the silent kind. Most of the prayer in these last days has been one person, alone. Here the silence is shared.
screen: `BENCHES FACING EACH OTHER.` → `A WOMAN STANDS, SPEAKS, SITS.` → `A HANDSHAKE ENDS IT.`

segments.voice: Quakers call themselves the Religious Society of Friends. Their founder, an Englishman named George Fox, wrote a letter to fellow ministers that carries today's line. He urges them to live in a way that preaches without words, and then, he says, "you will come to walk cheerfully over the world, answering that of God in every one." Hold that phrase up four ways. First, why silence. As Friends see it, if there is something of God in every person, then nobody needs to stand in between. So in the silent kind of meeting there's no planned sermon and no appointed speaker. Friends wait together, listening inward. Second, when someone speaks. Anyone may stand, a child, a visitor, a longtime member, if they feel moved to. Friends call this ministry. It's meant to come out of the silence, not out of a prepared speech, and it's usually short. After it, no one debates it. The silence takes it back. Third, that of God in every one. Notice the word Fox uses: answering. Not just finding something holy in other people, but responding to it, meeting it. Friends have read that phrase as a call to treat every person as someone who can hear God directly, which has shaped how they handle disagreement, decisions, and conflict. Fourth, not every meeting is silent. Friends differ. Some Quaker meetings have pastors, hymns and sermons; others, like the one in our hook, gather in silence. Both are Quaker. And the handshake at the end? It's simply how a silent meeting knows it's over.
screen: `A LETTER FROM GEORGE FOX.` · `NOBODY STANDS IN BETWEEN.` · `SPEAK ONLY WHEN MOVED.` · `NOT EVERY MEETING IS SILENT.` · then, large: `ANSWERING THAT OF GOD IN EVERY ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in silence with others. If someone is near you right now, a partner, a roommate, a stranger on the bus, let your silence include them. If you're alone, bring a few people to mind, and sit with them as if the bench were facing you. Don't send them advice. Just wait together, listening. If a word rises that feels worth saying, you can hold it. Not every word needs to be spoken. The bell holds the time.
Quaker silence. Friends waiting together without a planned sermon, speaking only when moved, trusting that something of God is in every one. Today's word.
Your line: that of God in every one. Today, pick one person who's hard for you, and look for one thing in them worth answering. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: In unprogrammed Quaker meetings, Friends gather in silence, anyone may stand to speak briefly when moved, and the meeting ends with handshakes; programmed Friends meetings include pastors, hymns and sermons.
